option_a: retain your continuous memory and sense of self but discover that every choice you have ever made was fully determined by prior causes, leaving no room for genuine agency
option_b: possess real, undetermined free will and full moral responsibility for every consequence of every choice, but lose all memory of who you were before the age of twelve
framing: Whether the self is constituted by continuity of memory or by the authenticity of choice.

option_a: know with certainty that consciousness is purely physical — that your sense of inner experience is an emergent property of neurons and nothing more
option_b: know with certainty that consciousness is non-physical — that your mind exists independently of your brain, but that this fact cannot be scientifically demonstrated or shared with anyone
framing: Whether it is better to have a true but reductive account of the self, or a transcendent one that must remain forever private.

option_a: live in a world where every moral question has a single correct answer, discoverable through reason — but you are personally constitutionally unable to reach the right answer more than half the time
option_b: live in a world where moral truth is genuinely plural and context-dependent — but you have unusually refined moral perception and your judgments are almost always the wisest in the room
framing: Whether moral objectivity or moral competence matters more to living ethically.

option_a: prevent a serious injustice from occurring but only by committing a small injustice yourself — and no one, including you, will ever know you did it
option_b: refuse to commit the small injustice, allowing the larger one to happen — and carry the private knowledge that you could have stopped it
framing: Whether moral integrity is about the outcome of your actions or the cleanliness of your hands.

option_a: live four hundred years, watching everyone you love die, outlasting every institution and culture you were raised in, unable to form attachments that will survive your lifespan
option_b: live a single concentrated decade of extraordinary depth — profound love, meaningful work, genuine understanding — and then cease to exist entirely
framing: Whether the value of a life is measured by its duration or its intensity.

option_a: remember every moment of your life with perfect fidelity — every embarrassment, every loss, every version of yourself you have since outgrown — unable to forget anything
option_b: lose all autobiographical memory every seven years, retaining skills and knowledge but beginning each cycle as a stranger to your own past
framing: Whether personal identity requires narrative continuity or whether it can be renewed in cycles.

option_a: have access to a complete and true account of every fact about the physical universe, but lose the ability to form new beliefs — you will know everything knowable, but you are done learning
option_b: retain the full capacity for curiosity, wonder, and discovery, but know that every answer you find will open three new questions and that complete understanding is permanently out of reach
framing: Whether knowledge is valuable as a destination or only as a process.

option_a: be the person who discovers the most important scientific truth of the next century — one that reshapes how humanity understands itself — but the discovery leads directly to a technology that causes enormous harm
option_b: spend your life doing careful, unspectacular work that prevents a catastrophe no one will ever know was coming, and receive no recognition because the disaster never happened
framing: Whether the moral weight of knowledge lies in its truth or its consequences.

option_a: experience your life as it is, with full uncertainty about whether other people have genuine inner lives or are philosophical zombies — and this uncertainty can never be resolved
option_b: know with certainty that every person you meet is fully conscious and has an inner life as rich as yours — but this knowledge comes with the permanent inability to ever feel alone
framing: Whether the mystery of other minds is a burden or a necessary condition for genuine connection.

option_a: live in a society that is perfectly just by every measurable standard — equal outcomes, no exploitation, no poverty — but one you had no hand in designing and cannot meaningfully change
option_b: live in a genuinely imperfect society that you helped build, whose flaws you understand, and whose direction you can still influence through your choices
framing: Whether justice is something to inhabit or something to pursue — and whether the pursuit is itself part of the good life.
